en: The Sūtra on the Wife of the Householder Dharmadatta, translated by an unknown person, now appended to the Liang Records.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with...
There were one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattvas present.
At dawn, the Buddha donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food, with the bhikṣus and bodhisattvas all attending upon him as his retinue.

The devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, mountain deities, and the kings of the gandharvas all scattered flowers and burned incense; they played various musical instruments and sang praises of the Buddha’s virtues, reciting these verses:
"Throughout countless billions of kalpas, You have accumulated practices beyond measure.
Out of compassion for all living beings, You cause them to resolve upon the Great Path."
The three realms are like a magical illusion; all things are entirely empty and non-existent.
One who can clearly understand this wisdom shall deliver and liberate all throughout the ten directions.
With the brilliance of the thirty-two marks and the excellence of the eighty secondary characteristics, they shine forth.
From his mouth issue ten trillion sounds, and his merit naturally adorns his countenance.
Though he dwells within the three realms, he reveals the three sites of enlightenment;
the three defilements are now extinguished, and the calamities of the three periods of time are removed.
"The mind is like a bright moon-jewel; dwelling amidst desires, it remains unattached.
Walking with equanimity, it is free from love and hate; toward all things, there is neither preference nor aversion.

Thereupon, the people heard this song praising the Buddha’s virtues. The entire nation gathered to observe the Buddha’s coming and going; his every movement and gesture was calm and composed. His majestic countenance was like the moon among the stars, or like the sun first rising, illuminating the whole world without any obstruction.

He is like the Brahma King dwelling among the gods, or like Śakra, Lord of Devas, who is the most honored among the gods in the Trāyastriṃśa palace; he is like Mount Sumeru appearing within the great ocean, stable and immovable amidst the four continents, before whom all rejoice, leap for joy, and pay homage with palms joined.
When the Buddha arrived outside the gate of the elder Fa-zhi’s residence and proceeded into the inner chamber, he emitted a great radiance that illuminated the ten directions.

At that time, the elder’s wife had prepared and adorned her couch; she embellished her body with various precious necklaces and wore sandalwood incense and facial cosmetics, her countenance radiant with five colors as if it were eternal.
Whenever his male and female slaves committed even the slightest transgression, he would beat them with cruel severity without inquiring into the right or wrong of the matter.
Seeing from afar the Buddha’s brilliance surpassing the light of the sun, he thought to himself:

"This radiance is not of the same kind as the light of the sun, moon, Śakra, Brahmā, or the various devas; it is pure, cool, tranquil, and immeasurable. My body has been graced by it and is entirely free from affliction; I am neither hungry nor thirsty, but naturally satiated. Why, then, do I inflict the scourge upon my servants?"

She hurried toward the gate and beheld the World-Honored One; his marks and signs were radiant beyond compare, his faculties were tranquil and composed without decline, like a mountain of the seven treasures, shining and majestic. Overcome with shame, fear, sorrow, and joy, she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“I repent my transgressions and misfortunes; what I have committed is unfathomable. Being a woman, I was unable to reproach myself, for my anger and joy were driven by others.”
"Now I confess my transgressions and dare not conceal them.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent!"
Excellent!

You have attained a great benefit and escaped all decline; seeing the faults and calamities of your own body, you reform the past and cultivate the future. A human body is difficult to obtain, and the Buddha’s sutras are difficult to encounter, appearing only once in hundreds of millions of eons.
Why is it that one falls into a female body?

It is because within that state, there is the posture of lustful desire; one cannot cultivate the body or restrain the mind, allowing them to run wild, being full of jealousy and loquacity, and coveting physical appearance while relying on it for self-importance.

The world is impermanent; wealth, nobility, and power last but a moment. One should regard all those of lower station as one’s own infants. Nobility, wealth, poverty, and meanness are like the waxing and waning of the moon, or like the rising and setting of the sun, or the emergence of water, fire, and wind—they do not endure but soon decay. All things, whether monastic or lay, arise from the mind.
The heavens, the human realm, hell, the hungry ghosts, and the animal realm—all these arise from oneself alone;
so too it is with the Buddhas, the Gods among Gods, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas.
"Now this body of mine, with its thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, perceives clearly throughout the ten directions, all through thorough understanding and penetration.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the woman was filled with immeasurable joy; she again took refuge in him, reproaching her own ignorance and lamenting that she had only received what was insufficient, having failed to be transformed by the unsurpassed teachings she had not yet heard.
The Buddha said:
"The meaning of practicing the ten wholesome paths is as follows:

the body refrains from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; the mouth refrains from false speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, and harsh speech; and the mind refrains from covetousness, malice, and delusion."
One should practice the six perfections:
giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-minded concentration, and wisdom.
One should abide by the four immeasurable minds:
Through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—extending universal and great pity—he personally attained the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

Yet he acted as a slave, a servant, or a laborer, instructing them in the hardships of suffering, the cycle of birth and death, and the retribution of sin and merit, while showing them the perils and tribulations of the three miserable realms.
Admonishing them with the prohibitions of the Way and matters of righteous principle is superior to beating them with a staff.
"There are four matters for adorning oneself with necklaces. What are these four?
First is profound faith;
second is the observance of precepts;
third is samādhi.
The fourth is wisdom. These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva adorns themselves, conceiving of the Mahāyāna in their mind.

They perceive that there is neither male nor female, for all are like magical illusions; they understand that what a painter creates is accomplished at will according to his intent. Being thoroughly awakened to the wisdom of emptiness—that all things are fundamentally pure—they attain the nameless body and the four fearlessnesses, requiring no protection in these four matters. Thus, they walk alone through the three realms, delivering and liberating all beings.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching, the woman’s mind was opened and she leaped with joy; she immediately resolved to attain the unsurpassed, true, and perfect path and established herself on the stage of non-retrogression.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came to stand behind the Buddha and said to the woman:

“The path of the Buddha is difficult to attain; it would be better for you to seek to transform this female body into a male one, or to become a sun god, a moon god, a lord of the devas, or a wheel-turning sage king.”
Thereupon, the woman spoke in verse:

"The Lord of Devas, the Sun, the Moon, and Kings, As well as the Wheel-turning Monarchs, lords of the four quarters— Their power and majesty endure but a short while; They cannot be relied upon for long."
Wealth is like morning dew; what is seen in a dream vanishes suddenly upon waking, with no knowledge of where it has gone.
The five aggregates are like illusions and transformations; the three realms are created by oneself.
The three periods of time are equal; the mind of the Way has no peer.
Having understood this through true insight, who is male and what is female?
When the Lord of Devas heard these words, he remained silent and said nothing more.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent! Excellent!”

Just as you have said, the three realms are like illusions, transformations, echoes, mirages, the moon in water, and plantain trees; yet worldly people do not understand this and falsely reckon them to possess a self, thereby relying upon the triple world and being unable to save themselves.
The woman’s mind was immediately liberated and she transformed into a man; leaping into the air, she descended to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha said to her:

"In a future age, after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, you shall attain Buddhahood, to be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—named Vimalarāja (Stainless King), the God among Gods, whose world shall call him Prabhāśuddha (Pure Radiance)."
At that time, the countless thousands of devas and humans gathered there, seeing this miraculous response, all conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect enlightenment.
Then the wife of the elder and all her subordinates came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One, was our humble status originally different from what it is now?"
The Buddha said:
"All things are fundamentally non-existent; they exist only according to what the mind conceives.
Even if one serves as a lowly messenger, if one resolves to attain the Way, one can achieve Buddhahood."
Having attained such honor and magnificence, one indulges in arrogance and pride, remaining unable to escape the realms of the evil destinies—namely hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Just as the moon waxes and wanes and trees flourish and decay, all things are impermanent and not a single one can be relied upon; only the profound wisdom of the Way can ensure permanence, like space, which neither advances nor recedes.

At that time, the low-ranking messengers leaped for joy and, with great delight, resolved upon the Great Way; they transformed into men and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

“The five aggregates have no location, the six sense faculties have no root, and the twelve links of dependent origination have no beginning. The four great elements are but temporary conditions; what, then, is this ‘person’?”
When the Buddha had spoken thus, all were filled with joy.
The Sūtra on the Wife of the Elder Dharmadatta.
